source.title: Claims: TĀ 1/181-182 distinguishes two aspects of cognition — object
source.author: Codex/Hermes loop

claims.claim_text: In TĀ 1/181-182, Abhinavagupta distinguishes two aspects of cognition: the objective ascertainment (niścaya) that 'this has been perceived,' and the subjective awareness (pratipatti) that 'I perceive.' He argues the subjective awareness does not arise from a subsequent mental act (vikalpa) but from 'oneness with thought-free consciousness (avikalpa).' This parallels Dignāga's grāhyākāra/grāhakākāra distinction but grounds the two aspects in a prior non-dual consciousness rather than treating them as intrinsic features of cognition.
claims.hetu: the two aspects of cognition (objective ascertainment and subjective awareness) are distinguished but both arise from a pre-conceptual ground
claims.sadhya: the two-appearance structure of cognition is not self-grounding but depends on a prior non-dual consciousness
claims.vyapti_statement: If the subjective awareness arises from oneness with thought-free consciousness, then the two-aspect structure of cognition is not fundamental but derivative.

falsifier.condition: Show that Abhinavagupta's distinction between objective ascertainment and subjective awareness is merely a restatement of Dignāga's two-appearance doctrine with no substantive difference — i.e., that 'avikalpa' is equivalent to the co-arising of two appearances.
